questions.stem: A payroll job queue skips a job when an equal one is already pending: `if (!pending.contains(job)) pending.add(job);`. The team replaces its `PayoutJob(employeeId, month)` records with `Runnable` lambdas such as `() -> payroll.pay("e-212", "2026-03")`, and a double click now enqueues the same payout twice through two lambdas written the same way in two click handlers, each capturing the handler's `payroll` field. What reaches the queue?

options.text: One job, since both lambdas call the same method with the same arguments
options.says: a lambda has no equals of its own, so two lambdas with the same body are two different objects; the page's run printed `lambdas equal: false`

options.text: One job, since the queue compares the arguments each lambda captured
options.says: captured variables can't be read from outside the lambda, so nothing can compare them

options.text: Two jobs, since each lambda is an object that equals only itself
options.says: lambdas don't override equals, so contains() finds no equal job and both are added; a record compares its fields

options.text: Two jobs, since a queue of Runnable objects doesn't compare its elements with equals
options.says: contains() does call equals; it is the lambda's identity-based equals that lets the duplicate in

origin.section: A Command Is a Request Held as an Object, So It Can Be Queued, Logged and Run Again

questions.stem: A drawing app's `RecolorAll` command saves `before = new ArrayList<>(canvas.shapes())` in `execute()`, then calls `setColor(RED)` on every shape. `Shape` is a class with `getColor()` and `setColor(...)`. `undo()` calls `canvas.replaceShapes(before)`, which clears the canvas's list and adds the saved shapes. A user recolors three blue shapes and presses undo. What do they see?

options.text: Three blue shapes, since the saved list holds copies of the shapes made before setColor
options.says: new ArrayList copies the list, not its elements; the saved list holds the same Shape objects that setColor changed

options.text: Three blue shapes, since replaceShapes puts the saved shapes back on the canvas
options.says: the saved shapes are the recolored objects, so putting them back restores nothing

options.text: Three red shapes, since setColor changed the same shape objects the saved list holds
options.says: copying a list doesn't copy its elements; every mutable level needs its own copy, or the elements must be immutable

options.text: Three red shapes, since the saved list is the same list object the canvas holds and updates
options.says: new ArrayList<>(...) is a separate list, unlike a saved reference to the canvas's list; it is the shared Shape objects that stay red

origin.section: Undo Restores What the Command Saved, So It Must Save a Copy Taken When It Runs

questions.stem: An order service submits `reserve("SKU-88", 3)` to the inventory client as a `Callable`, waits with `future.get(1, SECONDS)`, gets a `TimeoutException`, calls `future.cancel(true)` and tells the user the reservation failed. The user clicks Reserve again and gets a confirmation. Can the inventory now hold six units for this user?

options.text: No, since cancel(true) stops the first request before it can reach the inventory
options.says: cancel(true) interrupts a local thread; a request already sent may have reached the inventory and been applied

options.text: No, since the TimeoutException shows the first request never reached the inventory
options.says: a TimeoutException only says the caller stopped waiting; the request may have arrived and been applied

options.text: Yes, since cancel(true) interrupts a local thread and can't undo the inventory's work
options.says: after a timeout the first request may have been applied, and cancel(true) only interrupts a local thread; the retry without a key adds a second reservation

options.text: Yes, since the TimeoutException shows the first request reached the inventory first
options.says: a TimeoutException says nothing about where the request got to; it may never have arrived, so six is possible but not shown by the timeout

origin.section: A Command That Timed Out May Still Have Run, So a Blind Retry Runs It Twice

questions.stem: A mobile banking app sends transfers with an `Idempotency-Key` header, and the server keeps the keys it has seen with their results. One transfer's first reply is lost, the client retries, and the money moves twice. Where is the likeliest cause?

options.text: In the client, since it sent the retry under the first key instead of a fresh one
options.says: reusing the first key is what lets the server answer the retry from its store; a fresh key makes it a new transfer

options.text: In the client, since it created a new key for the retry instead of reusing the first
options.says: the key names the request, not the attempt: created once where the user asked, reused on every attempt; a new key looks like a new transfer

options.text: In the server, since it should match a retry to its transfer by the request body
options.says: matching on content would merge two real transfers of the same amount; the key is what identifies the request

options.text: In the server, since a key it keeps can't stop a retry that comes after a lost reply
options.says: a stored key is exactly what covers a retry after a lost reply: the retry finds the stored result; the server-side failures the page names (a non-atomic check, an apply that throws after the money moved) are not this one

origin.section: An Idempotency Key Created With the Command Makes the Retry Safe
